When people say things like my ex

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

vignette:
Priya was thirty-two when it happened, though the memory still landed in her body with the same visceral force as if no time had passed at all. She had been alone in the apartment she shared with her then-boyfriend, a man whose casual cruelty had escalated over two years into something she had been too ashamed to name. That evening, he came home in a rage over a text message from a male coworker, and within minutes the argument turned physical. He pinned her to the bedroom floor, and as he forced himself on her, she could hear her own voice screaming "no" from somewhere far away, a sound that didn't seem to belong to her. At one point she caught a glimpse of her own face in the mirror across the room and did not recognize the person staring back. Afterwards, he told her it was her fault, that she had provoked him, and in the hollow silence that followed, she began to believe him. She never reported it. She told no one. A few weeks later she ended the relationship and moved out, convinced that if she just buried the whole thing deep enough, she could start over.

She married a kind man three years later, opened a small convenience store in a working-class neighborhood, and for a while the routine of ordering stock, running the register, and bagging groceries kept the worst of it at bay. But the memory refused to stay buried. It returned not as a coherent story she could tell herself-she had never been able to put the event into words, could not find sentences that captured the horror without sounding melodramatic or, worse, as if she were making excuses-but as raw sensory fragments: the pressure of his hand on her throat, the smell of his sweat, the way the ceiling light left a brownish afterimage on her vision. When the memory surfaced, it brought the same terror she had felt that night, a flooding, suffocating panic that made her feel as though she were back on the floor with him above her. And it brought guilt-a deep, corrosive certainty that she could have stopped it if she had been stronger, if she had left him sooner, if she had screamed louder. She spent hours in the back room of her shop, after closing, replaying the night in her mind and wondering how her life would have been different if the event had never occurred. She might still be carefree. She might trust people. She might not flinch when customers entered the store.

The triggers multiplied. She found herself avoiding public transport altogether, driving even when parking was impossible, because on a bus or a train she could not control who sat beside her or how close they stood. Certain names made her freeze-an old friend named Raj, a news report mentioning a woman with the same surname as her ex. When anyone at the shop said "my ex" in casual conversation, her stomach dropped and she had to excuse herself to the stockroom. And she became hypervigilant to women who reminded her of other victims. She had learned, years after the assault, that her ex had hurt another woman before her-a college classmate with a round face and long black hair. Now, whenever a customer who fit that description walked into her store, Priya's throat tightened, her palms went slick, and she had to fight the urge to run. Her shop, which was supposed to be her sanctuary, became a place where she was constantly on guard. She positioned the checkout counter so that her back was against the wall at all times; she could see every aisle, every entrance. Sudden movements from customers-someone reaching quickly for a bag of chips, a child darting past-sent a jolt of alarm through her chest, and she would brace herself as if for an attack.

Her response to perceived threat had become automatic and deeply ingrained. When she felt unsafe, she became overly compliant-nodding too eagerly, smiling too broadly, agreeing with people she should have contradicted. A pushy customer could make her give them a discount they hadn't asked for. A man standing too close at the counter would get her meek apology instead of a request to step back. She hated herself for it afterward, but in the moment it felt like the only way to survive, a learned posture from years of placating her ex in the hope that he would stop. Her marriage suffered. Her husband noticed she would not let him sit behind her on the couch; she insisted on facing the door even at restaurants. He did not know the full story-she had told him only that she had been in a bad relationship-and she could not bring herself to say more because the words would not come.

What finally brought her to seek help was a flashback so vivid that she collapsed behind the counter during a quiet afternoon. Her husband found her curled on the floor, gasping, unable to speak. He drove her straight to a clinic, and she sat in the waiting room with her back pressed against the wall, convinced that anyone who walked through the door could be him. She is terrified that her mind will never let this go, that she is broken beyond repair. But she is also, for the first time, willing to admit that she cannot keep living like this-hypervigilant in her own store, guilt-ridden in her own home, silent about the event that rewired her entire nervous system. When the intake worker asked what she hoped for, she whispered, "I just want to be able to breathe without wondering if he's coming back."
